newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria says worst over for economy, sees growth.
newsitem.headline: Algeria says worst over for economy, sees growth.

text.p: Algeria said it has pulled its economy out of eight successive years of stagnation to achieve steady growth rates, with the last two years showing a positive performance and strong growth forecast in 1997.
Finance Minister Abdelkrim Harchaoui said the government expects gross domestic product to rise by a real 5.0 percent this year against four percent in 1996 and 3.8 percent in 1995.
"The conditions to relaunch the economy have been met," he said in an interview.
Harchaoui said inflation would be an average nine percent in 1997 compared to 18 percent last year and 29.8 percent in 1995.
"This is a very significant indicator of performance to encourage investment and the financing of the economy," he told Reuters.
Harchaoui said there were also improvements on the balance of trade, with Algeria achieving a $4.2 billion trade surplus in 1996 compared to a deficit of $0.9 billion in 1995.

Harchaoui said the 1996 trade surplus was due mainly to higher oil prices. The government had budgeted for an average oil price of $17 a barrel but had then earned $21.5 a barrel. The surplus was also boosted by a record cereals harvest of 5.0 million tonnes against an average of 2.0 million tonnes.
The country's foreign exchange reserves were $4.2 billion in 1996 compared to $2.11 billion in 1995 and stood at $5.3 billion in February 1997, the equivalent of six months import cover.
Algeria's improving economy, achieved while fighting a five-year war against Moslem insurgents, was increasingly recognised abroad, he said.

"The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, which monitor regularly the performance of the Algerian economy, not only recognise that Algeria has reached their performance criteria but they also recognise that the country has performed beyond these criteria," he said.
Algeria signed a three-year accord with the IMF in 1995 to reform its economy after the North African country reached a debt rescheduling with its foreign creditors.
Foreign debt stood at $31.5 billion in 1996 against $31.2 billion in 1995, Harchaoui said.
Foreign debt would be kept at around $32 billion in 1997. The cost of servicing these loans would represent 35 percent of the country's export earnings compared to 90 percent in 1993.

"At the end of 1993 we were in the eighth year of negative gross domestic product growth. The economy was virtually stagnant with a very poor added value to meet the economic problems facing the country and a level of foreign debt stifling the economy," he said.
The rescheduling deal that same year changed everything.

"With this programme we achieved the whole package of performance criteria, particularly cutting the budget deficit, bringing credit for the economy under control, the money supply, reducing the inflation rate and markedly improving macro -economic balances and financial stability.

"This performance is extraordinary for an economy emerging from readjustment after a deep crisis which lasted a decade because of the collapse of oil prices since 1986 which slashed practically half of Algeria's export earnings," Harchaoui added.
